fieldworkDocument.title: Measgaichte / Miscellaneous
fieldworkDocument.note: [NOTES: some notes added (most probably by K. D. MacDonald?). See below for details.]

item.description: a fetter for dogs or animals in general. [NOTES: note added above ‘t’ in ‘ti’ – d.]
the last word here means ‘scruffy’. [NOTES: note added – (placename).]
too much fertiliser put on potatoes.
an earmark.
an earmark. Same shape as the needle used to mend nets.
earmark where the top of the ear is rounded.
the orifice of the gullet which swells when you have a cold. [NOTES: ‘chir’ corrected to ‘chìr’ and note added – (= chìoch shlugain?).]
a workmanlike person. [NOTES: corrected to ‘conabhair’.]
boisterous, shouting person.
an untidy person.
making sure that the water is not too deep before wading ashore. [NOTES: ‘grunn’ corrected to ‘grunn(d)’.]
tight lipped. [NOTES: note added – (= glas ghuib?).]
black magic.
“Tha i air a dhol far na fuidhean.” – when something has gone to extremities. Also applied to someone who has been drinking excessively.
a drop of milk or water. Usually heard as – “Cha robh spannadh bainne aice.”
head of the household.
rafters running across the roof to the ‘maide feannaig’.
bit of wood that ran across the couples.
a fragment of a rainbow seen in the morning. Indicative of bad weather. [NOTES: note added – (= fadadh-cruaidh).]
a circle round the moon indicating bad weather. [NOTES: ‘buaille’ corrected to ‘buaile’.]
a pulled muscle. [NOTES: ‘feithe’ corrected to ‘fèithe’.]
the root of a boil. [NOTES: ‘mathair’ corrected to ‘màthair’.]
a well built, chubby man.
applied in the sense of something that was rare, i.e. “Dh’ith mi nith gun riaghailt an diugh.” – referring to a rare treat such as ‘ceann cròpaig’. [NOTES: ‘nith’ corrected to ‘nì’.]
someone without speech. [NOTES: Mr O’Henley added what appears to be a ‘j’ above ‘d’ in ‘deamadh’ – to show pronunciation?] [NOTES: note added – “Bha e na shuidhe gun deamadh.”]
goalkeeper.
applied to people who were engaged in slandering each other. [NOTES: note added above ‘raoin’ – Bha iad a’ rùin.]
a weaveress.
shin.
smithereens.
refers to people or animals running amok. “Ruith iad…”
headquarters.
another word for “sùil chruthaich”.
sitting cross legged.
equivalent of a bushel.
a bottle of whisky. Leth bodach – a half bottle.
grey, wissened [sic] [wizened?] look.
a patch of sand on a rocky coastline. [NOTES: corrected to ‘goirtein’.]
a fit which hit cows or sheep. [NOTES: corrected to ‘neafain’.]
a witch.
doorstep. [NOTES: ‘sgiùraid’ corrected to ‘sgliùraid’.]
witch.
witch.
“Seilecheag air talamh toll, clacharan air lic luim, searrach sean làir ’s a thonn rium, dh’aithnich mi nach rachadh a’ bhliadhna rium.” [NOTES: ‘sean’ corrected to ‘seann’ and ‘thonn’ to ‘thòn’.]
an indication of bad weather, when mist and a full moon were visible simultaneously.
when two suns were visible. Indicated bad weather.
a large crag, rock. [NOTES: corrected to ‘brèineard’.]
shimmering, glitter-like appearance in grass during an especially hot summer.
a plant seen on the moorland. If kicked or disturbed the petals gave off a smell which quickened the appetite. Therefore people were counselled to carry some form of food.
sorrel.
a length of iron, pointed at one end and used for holing corrugated iron. [NOTES: ‘biorr’ corrected to ‘bior’.]
a human affliction. Usually a combination of vomit and heartburn.
caterpillars. If eaten by cows their stomach would swell. Cured by eating snails. [NOTES: ‘bràtagan’ corrected to ‘bratagan’.]
salamander. Used to frighten children into doing what they were told to do. “Fhalbh dh’an leabaidh mu’n tig na corracha-cagailte.”
A’ cheum air dh’fhàg sinn – the unwilling step. [NOTES: ‘dh’fhàg’ corrected to ‘ghàg’.]
plover.
good weather. “Latha aighseach.” [NOTES: ‘aighseach’ corrected to ‘aibhseach’.]
a track or path used by cattle. [NOTES: note added – ùtraid.]
flock of birds.
the leg of a spade.
the blade of the spade.
sneaky fellow. [NOTES: corrected to ‘giungaire’.]
rough and ready.
a store, wealth of information, etc.
originating.
